lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use opposite leaves + small 5-part epigynous flowers + inferior ovary + drupaceous fruit, then split Sambucus from Viburnum by compound versus simple leaves and fruit-stone architecture.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas project-pool module across Sambucus and Viburnum
project_scope.note: The source pool has four rows but only three current species concepts because Sambucus nigra subsp. canadensis is a synonym of accepted Sambucus canadensis.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start at the node: both project genera have opposite leaves. Then inspect broad cymose or paniculate flower clusters with small usually regular 5-part flowers above an inferior ovary. Confirm with a fleshy drupaceous fruit.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Woody shrubs or small trees in the project pool. Sambucus has opposite pinnately compound leaves; Viburnum has opposite simple leaves.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers are typically small, epigynous and 5-merous, with a 5-lobed rotate to campanulate corolla and 5 stamens. Ovary is inferior.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Fleshy and drupaceous. Sambucus fruits contain several hard pyrenes; Viburnum commonly matures a one-stoned drupe.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Opposite leaves + broad cluster of small regular flowers + inferior ovary + drupe gets the family. Then compound leaf = Sambucus; simple leaf = Viburnum.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: opposite node → compound-vs-simple leaf → flat/broad flower cluster → inferior ovary → drupe/pyrenes → Caprifoliaceae tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: This is a nice visual family because the two project genera separate before you ever need a microscope: elder has compound leaves; viburnum has simple leaves.

steps.title: 1 · Start with the opposite node
steps.look_for: Leaves arising in opposite pairs on a woody stem.
steps.why_it_matters: The shared Dipsacales starting point gets you into the right neighborhood.

steps.title: 2 · Compound leaf? Think Sambucus
steps.look_for: A single opposite leaf divided into multiple leaflets along a rachis.

steps.title: 3 · Simple leaf? Think Viburnum
steps.photo_role: Viburnum rufidulum simple leaf + rusty bud/twig
steps.look_for: One undivided leaf blade per petiole; in rusty blackhaw, look for rusty hairs/scurf on buds, petioles or young surfaces.
steps.why_it_matters: Provides the local Viburnum door before flowering.

steps.title: 4 · Read the whole flower cluster
steps.look_for: Many small 5-part regular flowers arranged in a broad terminal cluster rather than a few large tubular flowers.
steps.why_it_matters: A useful contrast with many Lonicera flowers in Caprifoliaceae.

steps.title: 5 · Confirm the inferior ovary
steps.look_for: Perianth and stamens attached above the ovary.
steps.why_it_matters: Connects the family to its Dipsacales lineage and separates lookalikes with superior ovaries.

steps.title: 6 · Finish with the fruit stone pattern
steps.look_for: Sambucus fruit with several pyrenes versus Viburnum's typically single-stoned drupe.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit anatomy gives a durable genus tie-breaker after flowering.

steps.title: 7 · Taxonomy card: elderberry duplicate
steps.look_for: Sambucus nigra subsp. canadensis → accepted Sambucus canadensis; retain Sambucus nigra as a separate Old World species concept.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents the source pool from double-counting American elderberry.

comparisons.title: Viburnaceae vs Caprifoliaceae
comparisons.rule: Both often start with opposite leaves and inferior ovaries. Project Viburnaceae is entirely woody, with broad clusters of small regular flowers and drupaceous fruits. Caprifoliaceae includes tubular/zygomorphic honeysuckles and the herbaceous valerian dry-fruit lineage.

comparisons.title: Sambucus vs Lonicera
comparisons.rule: Sambucus has pinnately compound leaves and broad clusters of many small regular flowers; Lonicera has simple leaves and more conspicuous tubular/funnelform flowers.

comparisons.title: Viburnum vs Symphoricarpos
comparisons.rule: Both are opposite-leaved shrubs with fleshy fruits. Viburnum combines simple leaves with broad 5-part flower clusters and typically a one-stoned drupe; Symphoricarpos has smaller bell/funnel flowers and berry-like fruits with a different internal seed/nutlet plan.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not count Sambucus nigra subsp. canadensis as an additional current American elderberry taxon; current Kew synonymizes it under Sambucus canadensis.

part_specific_photo_handoff.formal: opposite pinnately compound leaf; rachis and leaflets
part_specific_photo_handoff.photo_role: whole leaf with node and leaflet attachments visible
part_specific_photo_handoff.caption_goal: Point out that several leaflets belong to one compound leaf; do not confuse leaflets with separate leaves.

part_specific_photo_handoff.plain: one undivided leaf and rusty fuzz
part_specific_photo_handoff.photo_role: matched leaf-node and young twig/bud macro
part_specific_photo_handoff.caption_goal: Compare one simple blade per petiole with elderberry's leaflets; inspect rusty hairs at high magnification.

part_specific_photo_handoff.plain: flower parts sit above seed-bearing swelling
part_specific_photo_handoff.caption_goal: Identify ovary position from floral insertion, not a front-view flower alone.

part_specific_photo_handoff.plain: several hard pieces versus one stone inside fruit
part_specific_photo_handoff.caption_goal: Count pyrenes in cut mature fruit, not from external fruit color.
